nodes.label: Unit 4 — The Circle
nodes.description: First geometry unit of the second term: circle definitions, positions of points/lines/circles, identifying a circle, and the relation between chords and the center.

nodes.label: Basic definitions: circle, center, radius, chord, diameter
nodes.description: Define the circle as the set of points of a plane at a constant distance (radius length) from a fixed point (center); classify points as inside, on, or outside the circle; define the surface of the circle, radius, chord, and diameter; congruent circles have equal radii.

nodes.label: The diameter as the longest chord; triangle-inequality arguments
nodes.description: Prove and apply that the diameter is the longest chord in a circle (diameter = 2r); use the triangle inequality with radii (e.g. MN + MD > ND with MD = MB) to compare lengths in circle figures.

nodes.label: Symmetry in the circle and the chord–center corollaries
nodes.description: Any straight line through the center is an axis of symmetry (infinitely many). Corollaries: (1) the line through the center and the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it; (2) the line through the center perpendicular to a chord bisects it; (3) the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center. Apply with the Pythagorean theorem to chords and parallel chords.

nodes.label: Position of a point with respect to a circle
nodes.description: For circle M with radius length r and point A in its plane: A is outside the circle iff MA > r, on the circle iff MA = r, inside iff MA < r (and vice versa); solve equations and inequalities on MA.

nodes.label: Position of a straight line with respect to a circle; tangents
nodes.description: With MA ⊥ L at A: the line is outside the circle iff MA > r, a secant (two common points) iff MA < r, a tangent (one common point) iff MA = r. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency; a line perpendicular to a diameter at an endpoint is a tangent.

nodes.label: Position of a circle with respect to another circle
nodes.description: For circles M, N with radii r1 > r2: distant iff MN > r1 + r2; touching externally iff MN = r1 + r2; intersecting iff r1 − r2 < MN < r1 + r2; touching internally iff MN = r1 − r2; one inside the other iff MN < r1 − r2 (concentric when MN = 0). The line of centers of touching circles passes through the point of tangency perpendicular to the common tangent; the line of centers of intersecting circles is perpendicular to the common chord and bisects it.

nodes.label: Identifying the circle through given points; the circumcircle
nodes.description: Infinitely many circles pass through one point, or through two points (centers on the axis of the segment; smallest radius = half the segment). One and only one circle passes through three noncollinear points; none through collinear points. The circumcircle of a triangle has its center at the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides.

nodes.label: Chord length versus distance from the center
nodes.description: Using (MX)² + (AX)² = r² for a chord with midpoint X: the closer the chord is to the center of the circle, the longer it is, and vice versa; compare chords and solve for unknown lengths.

nodes.label: Equal chords are equidistant from the center, and the converse
nodes.description: Theorem: chords of a circle equal in length are equidistant from the center (also in congruent circles). Converse: in the same circle or congruent circles, chords equidistant from the center(s) are equal in length. Applications to inscribed isosceles triangles.

questions.stem: The circle is the set of points of a plane which are at a constant distance from a fixed point in the same plane. The fixed point is called … and the constant distance is called …

choices.text: the center of the circle; the radius length
the center of the circle; the chord length

solution: By the definition of the circle, the fixed point is called the center of the circle.
The constant distance from the center to every point of the circle is called the radius length.
That is why we denote the circle by its center and say: circle M.
questions.source_note: Original question; definition of the circle, p.39

questions.stem: A line segment whose end points are any two points on the circle is called …
solution: The chord is a line segment whose end points are any two points on the circle.
A radius has only ONE endpoint on the circle (the other endpoint is the center), so it is not a chord.
A special chord that passes through the center is called a diameter.
questions.source_note: Original question; chord definition, p.40

questions.stem: For circle M with center M, which of the following statements is correct?

choices.text: $M \in$ circle M and $M \in$ surface of circle M
$M \notin$ circle M and $M \notin$ surface of circle M
$M \notin$ circle M and $M \in$ surface of circle M
$M \in$ circle M and $M \notin$ surface of circle M

solution: The circle is only the set of points at distance r from the center; the center itself is at distance 0 from itself, so $M \notin$ circle M.
The surface of the circle is the set of points of the circle $\cup$ the set of points inside the circle.
M is a point inside the circle, so $M \in$ surface of circle M.
questions.source_note: Original question; surface of the circle and drill 3 (M ∉ circle M, M ∈ …), p.40

questions.stem: If the radius length of circle M equals $7$ cm, find the diameter length in cm.
solution: The diameter is the chord passing through the center of the circle, so it is made of two radii.
Diameter length $= 2r = 2 \times 7$.
Diameter length $= 14$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original question; exercise 4 pattern (radius r → diameter 2r), p.41

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.text: Every chord of a circle is a diameter of it
Every diameter of a circle is a chord of it
Every radius of a circle is a chord of it
Two circles are congruent if their centers coincide

solution: The diameter is defined as the chord passing through the center of the circle — so every diameter is a chord, and B is correct.
A is wrong: a chord that does not pass through the center is not a diameter.
C is wrong: a radius has one endpoint at the center, not two endpoints on the circle.
D is wrong: two circles are congruent if their radii are equal in length — concentric circles can have different radii.
questions.source_note: Original question; definitions of radius/chord/diameter and congruent circles, p.40

questions.stem: The longest chord in a circle is …

choices.text: any chord perpendicular to the diameter

solution: The diameter of a circle is its largest chord in length.
Reason: for any chord AB not through the center, the triangle inequality in $\triangle AMB$ gives $AM + MB > AB$, and $AM + MB = 2r$ = diameter length.
So every other chord is shorter than the diameter.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 3 (diameter is the largest chord), p.40

questions.stem: The radius length of circle M is $6.5$ cm. Find the length in cm of the longest chord that can be drawn in circle M.
solution: The longest chord in a circle is the diameter.
Diameter length $= 2r = 2 \times 6.5 = 13$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original question; diameter as largest chord with numbers, p.40

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $r$, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord that does NOT pass through the center. Then $AB \; \square \; 2r$, where $\square$ is …
solution: Join $\overline{MA}$ and $\overline{MB}$; since the chord does not pass through M, the points A, M, B form a triangle.
By the triangle inequality in $\triangle AMB$: $AM + MB > AB$.
$AM = MB = r$ (radii), so $2r > AB$, i.e. $AB < 2r$.
questions.source_note: Original question; proof idea of drill 3 (AM + MC > AC pattern), p.40

questions.stem: In circle M, $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, D is a point on the circle, and N is a point on $\overrightarrow{BA}$ outside the circle. Drawing the radius $\overline{MD}$, which result follows?
solution: In $\triangle NMD$, the triangle inequality gives $MN + MD > ND$.
$MD = MB$ because both are radii of circle M.
Substituting: $MN + MB > ND$, and since M lies between N's side and B on the diameter line, $MN + MB = NB$.
Therefore $NB > ND$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (prove NB > ND via radius MD), p.41

questions.stem: The number of axes of symmetry of a circle is …
solution: Any straight line passing through the center of a circle is an axis of symmetry of it.
There is an infinite number of straight lines passing through the center.
So the circle has an infinite number of axes of symmetry.
questions.source_note: Original question; symmetry activity and Think question, p.42

questions.stem: In circle M, $\overline{MC} \perp \overline{AB}$ where $\overline{AB}$ is a chord and $C \in \overline{AB}$. Then C is …
solution: Corollary: the straight line passing through the center of a circle and perpendicular to any chord of it bisects this chord.
$\overline{MC}$ passes through the center M and is perpendicular to the chord $\overline{AB}$.
So C is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, i.e. $AC = CB$.
questions.source_note: Original question; important corollary (2), p.42

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $13$ cm, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of length $24$ cm. Find the distance in cm of the chord from the center M.
solution: Let X be the point where the perpendicular from M meets $\overline{AB}$; the line through the center perpendicular to a chord bisects it, so $AX = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ cm.
In the right-angled triangle $AXM$: $(MX)^2 + (AX)^2 = (AM)^2$.
$MX = 5$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 2 (radius 13, chord 24), p.43

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $10$ cm, a chord $\overline{CD}$ is at distance $6$ cm from the center. Find the length of $\overline{CD}$ in cm.
solution: Let X be the foot of the perpendicular from M on $\overline{CD}$; then X is the midpoint of the chord (corollary).
In the right-angled triangle $MXC$: $(CX)^2 = r^2 - (MX)^2 = 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64$, so $CX = 8$ cm.
$CD = 2 \times CX = 16$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original question; chord length from distance to center, pp.42-44

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two parallel chords in circle M lying on OPPOSITE sides of the center, $AB = 10$ cm, $CD = 24$ cm, and the radius length is $13$ cm. Find the distance in cm between the two chords.
solution: The perpendicular from M to two parallel chords lies on one straight line, meeting $\overline{AB}$ at its midpoint X and $\overline{CD}$ at its midpoint Y.
Distance of $\overline{AB}$: $(MX)^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$, so $MX = 12$ cm.
Distance of $\overline{CD}$: $(MY)^2 = 13^2 - 12^2 = 169 - 144 = 25$, so $MY = 5$ cm.
The chords are on opposite sides of the center, so the distance between them $= MX + MY = 12 + 5 = 17$ cm.
(If they were on the same side, the distance would be $12 - 5 = 7$ cm — that is why the drill asks whether there are other answers.)
questions.source_note: Original variant of the parallel-chords drill (AB=12, CD=16, r=10 → new numbers 10, 24, 13), p.44

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and A is a point in its plane where $MA = 4$ cm. Then A is …
solution: A point A is on circle M if and only if $MA = r$.
Here $MA = 4$ cm $= r$, so A is on the circle.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 1 (MA = 4 with r = 4), p.46

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and $MA = 2\sqrt{3}$ cm. Then A is …
solution: Compare $MA$ with the radius length: $MA = 2\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{12}$ and $r = 4 = \sqrt{16}$.
$\sqrt{12} < \sqrt{16}$, so $MA < r$.
$MA < r$ means A is located inside the circle.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 2 (MA = 2√3 with r = 4), p.46

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and $MA = 3\sqrt{2}$ cm. Then A is …
solution: $MA = 3\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{18}$ and $r = 4 = \sqrt{16}$.
$\sqrt{18} > \sqrt{16}$, so $MA > r$.
$MA > r$ means A is located outside the circle.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 3 (MA = 3√2 with r = 4), p.46

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and $MA =$ zero. Then …

choices.text: A coincides with the center M, so A is inside the circle
the position of A cannot be determined

solution: $MA = 0$ means the distance between A and M is zero, so the point A is the center M itself.
Since $MA = 0 < r = 4$, the point A (the center) is inside the circle.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 4 (MA = zero), p.46

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $5$ cm, A is a point in its plane and $MA = (2x - 3)$ cm. If A is located OUTSIDE the circle, then …
solution: Point A is located outside circle M, so $MA > r$, i.e. $MA > 5$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (MA = 2x − 3, A outside, r = 5), p.47

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $7$ cm, L is a straight line in its plane and $\overline{MA} \perp L$ at $A \in L$ with $MA = 7$ cm. Then L is …

choices.text: a tangent to the circle, and $L \cap$ circle M $= \{A\}$

solution: Compare the distance MA with the radius length: $MA = 7 = r$.
When $MA = r$, the straight line L is tangent to circle M, and it has exactly one common point with the circle: $L \cap$ the circle $= \{A\}$.
questions.source_note: Original question; positions of a line, case MA = r, p.47

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $7$ cm and the distance between its center and the straight line L is $MA = 4\sqrt{3}$ cm. Then L …

choices.text: is a secant, intersecting the circle in two points
is a tangent to the circle

solution: $MA = 4\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{48}$ and $r = 7 = \sqrt{49}$.
$\sqrt{48} < \sqrt{49}$, so $MA < r$.
When $MA < r$, the straight line L is a secant to the circle: $L \cap$ circle M $= \{C, D\}$, two points.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 1 (MA = 4√3 with r = 7), p.47

questions.stem: L is a tangent to circle M at the point A. Then the measure of the angle between L and the radius $\overline{MA}$ equals …
solution: Important fact: a tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at its point of tangency.
So $L \perp \overline{MA}$, and the measure of the angle between them is $90°$.
questions.source_note: Original question; important fact 1, p.48

questions.stem: $\overline{XY}$ is a tangent to circle M at X, the radius length is $5$ cm, and $MY = 13$ cm. Find the length of $\overline{XY}$ in cm.
solution: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency, so $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{XY}$ and $\triangle MXY$ is right-angled at X.
By the Pythagorean theorem: $(XY)^2 = (MY)^2 - (MX)^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$.
$XY = 12$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 2 (5, 12, 13 tangent figure), p.48

questions.stem: The straight line L intersects circle M of radius length $7$ cm in two points, and the distance from the center to L is $MA = (3x - 5)$ cm. Then …
solution: L intersects the circle in two points (a secant), so $MA < r$: $3x - 5 < 7$, giving $3x < 12$, i.e. $x < 4$.
MA is a distance, so $MA \geq 0$: $3x - 5 \geq 0$, giving $x \geq \dfrac{5}{3}$.
Together: $\dfrac{5}{3} \leq x < 4$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 4 (L intersects circle M, MA = 3X − 5, r = 7), p.47

questions.stem: Circles M and N have radii lengths $9$ cm and $4$ cm respectively, and $MN = 13$ cm. Then the two circles are …
solution: When $MN = r_1 + r_2$, the two circles are touching externally (one common point between the two centers).
questions.source_note: Original question; Example 3 case A (radii 9 and 4, MN = 13), p.51

questions.stem: Circles M and N have radii lengths $9$ cm and $4$ cm respectively, and $MN = 5$ cm. Then the two circles are …
solution: When $MN = r_1 - r_2$, the two circles are touching internally (one common point, the smaller circle inside the larger).
questions.source_note: Original question; Example 3 case B (radii 9 and 4, MN = 5), p.51

questions.stem: Circles M and N have radii lengths $8$ cm and $3$ cm respectively, and $MN = 6$ cm. Then the two circles are …

choices.text: intersecting, because $r_1 - r_2 < MN < r_1 + r_2$

solution: In this case the two circles are intersecting: they have two common points and a common chord.
questions.source_note: Original question; two-circle position rules (drill case 3), p.50

questions.stem: Two circles M and N of radii lengths $8$ cm and $5$ cm are touching externally. Find the distance $MN$ between their centers in cm.
solution: Two circles are touching externally when the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 3 (circles touching two-by-two, radii 8 and 5), p.52

questions.stem: M and N are two circles intersecting at A and B, $AM = 9$ cm, $AN = 12$ cm and $\overline{MA} \perp \overline{AN}$. Find the length of the common chord $\overline{AB}$ in cm.
solution: $\triangle MAN$ is right-angled at A, so $MN = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ cm.
The line of centers of two intersecting circles is perpendicular to the common chord and bisects it; let it cut $\overline{AB}$ at C.
$\overline{AC}$ is the height to the hypotenuse of the right triangle: $AC \times MN = AM \times AN$, so $AC = \dfrac{9 \times 12}{15} = 7.2$ cm.
$AB = 2 \times AC = 14.4$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 2 (AM = 6, AN = 8, MA ⊥ AN → new numbers 9, 12), p.53

questions.stem: The number of circles which pass through three noncollinear points is …
solution: There is one and only one circle which passes through three noncollinear points.
Its center is the intersection point of the axes (perpendicular bisectors) of the two segments joining the points, and this intersection is a single point.
questions.source_note: Original question; deduction box (one and only one circle), p.56

questions.stem: A and B are two given points. The centers of all the circles passing through both A and B are located on …
solution: If a circle passes through A and B, then $\overline{AB}$ is a chord in it.
The perpendicular bisector of any chord of a circle passes through the center of the circle.
So every such center lies on the axis of $\overline{AB}$ — and every point of the axis can serve as a center, giving an infinite number of circles.
questions.source_note: Original question; drawing a circle through two given points, p.55

questions.stem: A and B are two points where $AB = 8$ cm. Find in cm the radius length of the smallest circle that can be drawn passing through A and B.
solution: The radius length of the smallest circle that can be drawn to pass through the two points A and B equals $\dfrac{1}{2} AB$.
That smallest circle is the one taking $\overline{AB}$ itself as a diameter, centered at the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$.
Radius $= \dfrac{8}{2} = 4$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original question; deduction 2 (smallest circle through A and B), p.56

questions.stem: A, B and C are three collinear points. How many circles pass through the three points A, B and C together?
solution: The center of such a circle would have to lie on the axis $L_1$ of $\overline{AB}$ and on the axis $L_2$ of $\overline{BC}$.
When A, B, C are collinear, $L_1 \parallel L_2$, so $L_1 \cap L_2 = \phi$ — there is no possible center.
So no circle can be drawn passing through three collinear points.
questions.source_note: Original question; Notice box (collinear case, L1 ∥ L2), p.56

questions.stem: To locate the center of the circumcircle of triangle ABC (the circle passing through its vertices), we draw …

choices.text: the perpendicular bisectors of the sides; their intersection point is the center
the bisectors of the angles of the triangle

solution: The circle which passes through the vertices of a triangle is called the circumcircle of this triangle, and the triangle is said to be inscribed in the circle.
Corollary: the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle intersect at a point which is the center of the circumcircle.
Each vertex-pair (side) is a chord of the circumcircle, and the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center — so their common point is the center.
questions.source_note: Original question; corollaries 1 and 2 (circumcircle), p.57

questions.stem: In circle M, chord $\overline{AB}$ is at distance $3$ cm from the center and chord $\overline{CD}$ is at distance $5$ cm from the center. Then $AB \; \square \; CD$, where $\square$ is …
solution: Rule: the closer the chord is to the center of the circle, the longer its length is, and vice versa.
$\overline{AB}$ is at distance 3 cm, which is closer to the center than $\overline{CD}$ at 5 cm.
So $AB > CD$.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 1 (compare using > < =), p.58

questions.stem: In circle M, $AB = 8$ cm and $CD = 6$ cm are two chords, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$ and $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$. Then $MX \; \square \; MY$, where $\square$ is …
solution: The longer chord is the closer one to the center (the rule 'closer ⟺ longer' read in reverse).
$AB = 8 > CD = 6$, so $\overline{AB}$ is closer to the center than $\overline{CD}$.
MX is the distance of $\overline{AB}$ and MY is the distance of $\overline{CD}$, so $MX < MY$.
questions.source_note: Original question; drill 1 second/third figures pattern, p.58

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $13$ cm, chord $\overline{AB}$ is at distance $5$ cm from the center and chord $\overline{CD}$ is at distance $12$ cm. Find $AB - CD$ in cm.
solution: For a chord at distance d from the center, half the chord $= \sqrt{r^2 - d^2}$ (from $(MX)^2 + (AX)^2 = r^2$).
$AB - CD = 24 - 10 = 14$ cm — the closer chord (5 cm away) is indeed the longer one.
questions.source_note: Original question; constant expression (MX)² + (AX)² = r², p.58

questions.stem: In circle M, chord $\overline{CD} = (x + 2)$ cm is at distance $4$ cm from the center, and chord $\overline{AB} = 8$ cm is at distance $6$ cm from the center. Then …
solution: $\overline{CD}$ is at distance 4 cm and $\overline{AB}$ at 6 cm, so $\overline{CD}$ is closer to the center.
The closer the chord is to the center, the longer it is: $CD > AB$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 2 (MF < ME → CD > … with (X+1) cm chord), p.59

questions.stem: In circle M, $AB = CD$ are two chords, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$ and $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$. Then …
solution: Theorem: if chords of a circle are equal in length, then they are equidistant from the center.
MX and MY are the distances of the two chords from the center.
$AB = CD$, so $MX = MY$.
questions.source_note: Original question; theorem statement, p.59

questions.stem: In circle M, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$, $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$, $MX = MY$ and $YD = 7$ cm. Find the length of $\overline{AB}$ in cm.
solution: $\overline{MY}$ passes through the center perpendicular to the chord $\overline{CD}$, so it bisects it: $CD = 2 \times YD = 14$ cm.
Converse of the theorem: in the same circle, chords which are equidistant from the center are equal in length.
$MX = MY$, so $AB = CD = 14$ cm.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 1 (MX = MY, YD = 7 → AB), p.61

questions.stem: In circle M, the chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are equal in length. The distance of $\overline{AB}$ from the center is $(2x + 1)$ cm and the distance of $\overline{CD}$ from the center is $9$ cm. Find the value of $x$.
solution: If chords of a circle are equal in length, then they are equidistant from the center.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill B (equal chords with algebraic distances), p.60

questions.stem: Triangle ABC is inscribed in circle M with $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C)$. X is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{AC}$. Which chain of reasoning proves $MX = MY$?

choices.text: $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C) \Rightarrow AC = AB$ (equal chords) $\Rightarrow$ they are equidistant from the center $\Rightarrow MX = MY$
$m(\angle B) = m(\angle C) \Rightarrow BC = AB \Rightarrow MX = MY$
X is a midpoint $\Rightarrow MX = \dfrac{1}{2} AB = MY$
$MX = MY$ because every two distances from the center are equal

solution: In $\triangle ABC$: $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C)$, so the sides opposite to them are equal: $AC = AB$ (isosceles triangle).

$\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two chords of circle M, and X is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, so $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$ (line through the center and a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it) — MX and MY are the two chords' distances from the center.
If chords of a circle are equal in length, then they are equidistant from the center: $AB = AC \Rightarrow MX = MY$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the inscribed-triangle drill (m∠B = m∠C → MX = MY), p.61

questions.stem: Triangle ABC is inscribed in circle M, $\overline{MD} \perp \overline{AB}$, $\overline{ME} \perp \overline{AC}$, $MD = ME$ and $m(\angle B) = 70°$. Find $m(\angle A)$ in degrees.
solution: $MD$ and $ME$ are the distances of the chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ from the center, and $MD = ME$.
Converse of the theorem: chords which are equidistant from the center are equal in length, so $AB = AC$.
$\triangle ABC$ is isosceles, so $m(\angle C) = m(\angle B) = 70°$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of drill 3 (MD = ME, m∠B = 65° → m∠A; new angle 70°), p.61

visuals.caption: One circle, three names: a radius from the center, a chord joining two points, and the diameter — the chord through M.
Drawing circle M splits the plane into three point sets: inside, on the circle, and outside.
Join the chord's ends to M: the triangle says AM + MB > AB, so no chord can beat the diameter 2r.

visuals.question: q:geo1-1-2:004
visuals.caption: Draw the radius MD: triangle NMD gives MN + MD > ND, and since MD = MB, that means NB > ND.
Fold the circle along any line through M and the halves match — every line through the center is an axis of symmetry.
Drop the perpendicular from M to a chord — it always lands on the chord's midpoint (and the reverse holds too).

visuals.question: q:geo1-1-3:003
visuals.caption: Half the chord (12), the radius (13) and the distance MX make a right triangle — Pythagoras gives MX = 5.
Measure MA against the radius: shorter means inside, equal means on the circle, longer means outside.

visuals.question: q:geo1-2-1:002
visuals.caption: Put each distance MA on a line next to r = 4: below 4 is inside, exactly 4 is on, past 4 is outside.
When the distance from M to the line is less than r, the line cuts the circle in two points — a secant.
A tangent touches at exactly one point — and the radius to that point always meets it at 90°.

visuals.question: q:geo1-2-2:004
visuals.caption: Tangent ⊥ radius makes a right triangle: 5² + XY² = 13², so the tangent length is 12.

visuals.question: q:geo1-2-3:001
visuals.caption: Touching externally: MN equals the two radii added, and the line of centers passes through the touch point A.

visuals.question: q:geo1-2-3:002
visuals.caption: Touching internally: the small circle hugs the big one from inside and MN shrinks to r₁ − r₂.

visuals.question: q:geo1-2-3:005
visuals.caption: Two intersecting circles: the line of centers cuts the common chord AB at right angles and splits it in half.
Pick any center you like — a circle through the single point A always exists, so there are infinitely many.
Every circle through A and B has its center on the axis of AB — the smallest one uses AB as a diameter.

visuals.question: q:geo1-3-1:005
visuals.caption: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at one point M — the center of the one and only circumcircle.

visuals.question: q:geo1-4-1:001
visuals.caption: Two chords, one circle: the chord sitting closer to M is the longer one — always.

visuals.question: q:geo1-4-1:003
visuals.caption: Same radius 13 for both chords: (distance)² + (half chord)² = 13², so d = 5 gives 24 and d = 12 gives only 10.
Equal chords keep equal distance from the center — and chords at equal distance must be equal (the converse).

visuals.question: q:geo1-4-2:005
visuals.caption: MD = ME forces AB = AC, so the inscribed triangle is isosceles: base angles 70° each leave 40° at A.
